lead: A valve timing diagram shows when the inlet and exhaust valves of a four-stroke engine open and close, in crank angle degrees measured from TDC and BDC. Real engines do not open the valves exactly at the dead centres, because the gas has inertia and needs time to start and stop moving; opening early and closing late fills and empties the cylinder better. A port timing diagram shows the same thing for the ports of a two-stroke engine. Both are drawn as a circle that the crank sweeps, and both are standard exam sketches.
prereq: You need the four strokes and the three ports from four-stroke and two-stroke engines.

blocks.text: Draw a circle with TDC at the top and BDC at the bottom, and let the crank turn clockwise. A four-stroke cycle needs two turns, 720°CA, so the diagram is a spiral of two turns: the intake stroke runs TDC → BDC on the first turn, compression BDC → TDC, power TDC → BDC on the second turn and exhaust BDC → TDC. Angles are crank degrees, not cam degrees: the camshaft turns at half crank speed.

items: Inlet valve opens (IVO) before TDC, by the inlet lead, so it is already open when the piston starts down.
Inlet valve closes (IVC) after BDC, by the inlet lag: the moving column of charge keeps flowing in, the ram effect, even though the piston has begun to rise.
Exhaust valve opens (EVO) before BDC, by the exhaust lead: the burnt gas, still at 3 to 5 bar, rushes out (blowdown), so the piston need not push against high pressure on the exhaust stroke.
Exhaust valve closes (EVC) after TDC, by the exhaust lag: the outgoing gas keeps flowing and drags burnt gas out of the clearance space.

blocks.text: Inlet open period = inlet lead + 180° + inlet lag. Exhaust open period = exhaust lead + 180° + exhaust lag. Valve overlap = inlet lead + exhaust lag: the few degrees around TDC when both valves are open, so the outgoing exhaust helps draw in the fresh charge. The spark (SI) or the start of injection (CI) is marked on the same diagram near the end of compression, but it is not a valve event.

sections.h3: SI and CI valve timing compared

blocks.text: Both engines use the same four events in the same order; only the size of the angles and the reasons differ. Typical values (they vary with design and speed):

An SI engine is throttled. At idle the inlet manifold is at low pressure while the exhaust is at about atmospheric, so a large overlap lets burnt gas flow back into the inlet and the idle becomes rough. A high-speed SI engine still uses a fair overlap and a late inlet closing, because at high speed the gas inertia is large and they improve breathing.

A naturally aspirated CI engine has no throttle, but its high compression ratio leaves very little space between the piston crown and the valve heads at TDC, so the valves cannot stand far open there, and the inlet pressure is not above the exhaust pressure. It therefore uses a small overlap. A turbocharged diesel, whose inlet pressure is above its exhaust pressure, uses a larger overlap so that clean air scavenges the clearance volume and cools the exhaust valve.

sections.h3: Port timing in a two-stroke engine

blocks.text: In a piston-ported engine the piston edge is the valve, so each port opens and closes at angles fixed by the height of the port in the cylinder wall. The exhaust and transfer ports are uncovered as the piston nears BDC and covered as it rises, so their events are symmetric about BDC: the exhaust port opens, say, 60° before BDC and closes 60° after BDC. The exhaust port sits higher than the transfer port, so it opens first and closes last.

A piston-controlled inlet port is uncovered by the piston skirt as the piston nears TDC, so its events are symmetric about TDC. Reed valves and rotary valves make the inlet timing unsymmetric, which helps at low speed.

Two periods matter. The blowdown period, from exhaust opening to transfer opening, lets the cylinder pressure fall below the crankcase pressure, so fresh charge does not flow back into the crankcase. The period from transfer closing to exhaust closing is the price of symmetric ports: the exhaust stays open with no fresh charge entering, so some charge escapes. Port timing cannot be changed on a running engine; tuners change it by raising or lowering the port edges.

spec.aria: Two timing circles with TDC at the top and BDC at the bottom. Left: an inlet arc from 10 degrees before TDC to 40 degrees after BDC and an exhaust arc from 45 degrees before BDC to 10 degrees after TDC, overlapping at the top. Right: exhaust port arc 60 degrees each side of BDC, transfer arc 45 degrees each side of BDC and inlet arc 55 degrees each side of TDC.

examples.question: A four-stroke SI engine has the inlet valve opening 10° before TDC and closing 40° after BDC, and the exhaust valve opening 45° before BDC and closing 10° after TDC. Find the inlet open period, the exhaust open period and the overlap, and the duration of the overlap at 3000 rev/min.
steps: Overlap = inlet lead + exhaust lag = 10° + 10° = 20°CA, from 10° before to 10° after TDC.
At 3000 rev/min the crank turns 50 × 360 = 18 000° per second, so 1° takes 1/18 000 s = 0.0556 ms.
examples.answer: Inlet 230°CA, exhaust 235°CA, overlap 20°CA, which lasts 1.11 ms at 3000 rev/min.

examples.question: A crankcase-scavenged two-stroke engine has its exhaust port open 60° before BDC, its transfer port open 45° before BDC and its inlet port open 55° before TDC; all ports are piston controlled. Find the open period of each port, the blowdown period, and the time the exhaust stays open after the transfer port closes, at 3000 rev/min.
steps: Piston-controlled ports are symmetric about their dead centre. Exhaust: open 60° before BDC to 60° after BDC = 120°CA.
Blowdown, exhaust opening to transfer opening: 60° − 45° = 15°CA.
After the transfer port closes (45° after BDC) the exhaust stays open until 60° after BDC: 15°CA, the same 15° because of the symmetry.
At 3000 rev/min 1° = 0.0556 ms, so each 15° period lasts 0.83 ms and the exhaust is open for 120 × 0.0556 = 6.7 ms.
examples.answer: Exhaust 120°CA, transfer 90°CA, inlet 110°CA; blowdown 15°CA and post-transfer exhaust 15°CA, each 0.83 ms at 3000 rev/min.

traps: Crank degrees, not cam degrees: the 20°CA overlap of the first example is only 10° of camshaft rotation.
Overlap is already inside the inlet and exhaust periods; do not add it again.
Inlet lead is measured from TDC but inlet lag from BDC; likewise exhaust lead from BDC and lag from TDC. Mixing the reference points gives wrong periods.
Do not write that CI engines never have overlap. Naturally aspirated diesels use a small one; turbocharged diesels a larger one.
A piston-ported two-stroke diagram is symmetric about BDC for exhaust and transfer. Do not draw it with unequal lead and lag as for a four-stroke.

quiz.a: The crank angle near TDC, at the end of exhaust and start of intake, during which the inlet and exhaust valves are open together.

quiz.q: Why does the exhaust valve open before BDC?
quiz.a: So the burnt gas, still at a few bar, can blow down before the exhaust stroke begins; the piston then pushes against low pressure and the pumping work falls, at the cost of a little expansion work.

quiz.q: Why does the inlet valve close after BDC?
quiz.a: The column of charge in the inlet is moving fast and keeps flowing in by its inertia (the ram effect) for some degrees after the piston starts up, so a late closing traps more charge.

quiz.q: An engine has inlet opening 12° before TDC and closing 50° after BDC, and exhaust opening 40° before BDC and closing 15° after TDC. Find both open periods and the overlap.
A two-stroke’s exhaust port is open for 130°CA and its transfer port for 100°CA. Find the blowdown period.
quiz.a: Both are symmetric about BDC: exhaust opens 65° and transfer 50° before BDC, so blowdown = 65 − 50 = 15°CA.

quiz.q: Why is the overlap of an SI engine kept small for a smooth idle but larger in a high-speed engine?
quiz.a: At idle the throttled inlet is at low pressure, so burnt gas flows back into it during a long overlap and dilutes the charge. At high speed the gas inertia is large and a long overlap and late inlet closing fill the cylinder better.

quiz.q: Why does a turbocharged diesel use a larger overlap than a naturally aspirated one?
quiz.a: Its inlet pressure is above the exhaust pressure, so during overlap fresh air flows straight through the clearance space, sweeping out residual gas and cooling the exhaust valve and piston crown. Without boost the flow could reverse.

beyond: Most new car engines vary the valve timing with speed and load using cam phasers, and some vary the lift too. Late inlet closing, the Miller or Atkinson cycle, lowers the effective compression ratio and is used in hybrid petrol engines. Search for variable valve timing, Miller cycle and exhaust port tuning.
